claim: The liver is primarily composed of hepatocytes (HCs), endothelial cells (ECs), Kupffer cells (KCs), and hepatic stellate cells (HSCs).
source: The liver is the largest solid organ in the body and is primarily composed of hepatocytes (HCs), endothelial cells (ECs), Kupffer cells (KCs), and hepatic stellate cells (HSCs), which spatially interact and cooperate with each other to maintain liver homeostasis.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about liver composition in the abstract.

claim: HSCs are the major source of GDF2 and BMP10 in the liver.
source: Here, we generated mice with conditional deletion of Gdf2 (also known as Bmp9) and Bmp10 in different liver cell types and demonstrated that HSCs were the major source of GDF2 and BMP10 in the liver.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from conditional knockout mice in different liver cell types, as described in the abstract and demonstrated in Figure 1A.

claim: ALK1 is expressed on KCs and ECs but not on HCs and HSCs.
source: Using transgenic ALK1 (receptor for GDF2 and BMP10) reporter mice, we found that ALK1 is expressed on KCs and ECs other than HCs and HSCs
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from transgenic ALK1 reporter mice shown in Figure 1D.

claim: GDF2 and BMP10 secreted by HSCs promote the differentiation of KCs and ECs and maintain their identity.
source: GDF2 and BMP10 secreted by HSCs promote the differentiation of KCs and ECs and maintain their identity.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing loss of KC and EC markers in Gdf2/Bmp10HSC-KO mice, as shown in Figures 1E-G and Figure 2.

claim: Pdgfb expression was significantly upregulated in KCs and ECs after Gdf2 and Bmp10 deletion.
source: Pdgfb expression was significantly upregulated in KCs and ECs after Gdf2 and Bmp10 deletion, ultimately leading to HSCs activation and liver fibrosis.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data showing increased Pdgfb expression in liver tissues, ECs, and liver macrophages from Gdf2/Bmp10HSC-KO mice, as shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Deletion of Gdf2 and Bmp10 leads to HSC activation and liver fibrosis.
source: Pdgfb expression was significantly upregulated in KCs and ECs after Gdf2 and Bmp10 deletion, ultimately leading to HSCs activation and liver fibrosis.
evidence: This is supported by histological data showing increased collagen deposition (Figure 5B), increased expression of Desmin and type I collagen (Figure 5D), and increased collagen IV expression (Figure 5E).

claim: ECs express angiocrine factors such as BMP2, BMP6, Wnt2, and Rspo3 to regulate HC iron metabolism and metabolic zonation.
source: ECs express several angiocrine factors, such as BMP2, BMP6, Wnt2, and Rspo3, to regulate HC iron metabolism and metabolic zonation.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature (Planas-Paz et al., 2016; Yang et al., 2014; Canali et al., 2017; Koch et al., 2017) and by RNA-seq data showing expression of these factors in ECs.

claim: Angiocrine factors were significantly decreased in ECs from Gdf2/Bmp10HSC-KO mice.
source: We found that these angiocrine factors were significantly decreased in ECs from Gdf2/Bmp10HSC-KO mice, which further resulted in liver iron overload and disruption of HC zonation.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data showing decreased expression of Wnt2, Wnt9b, Rspo3, Bmp2, and Bmp6 in ECs from Gdf2/Bmp10HSC-KO mice, as shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Decreased angiocrine factors in ECs resulted in liver iron overload.
source: We found that these angiocrine factors were significantly decreased in ECs from Gdf2/Bmp10HSC-KO mice, which further resulted in liver iron overload and disruption of HC zonation.
evidence: This is supported by Prussian blue staining showing iron overload in five out of seven Gdf2/Bmp10HSC-KO mice, as shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Decreased angiocrine factors in ECs resulted in disruption of HC zonation.
source: We found that these angiocrine factors were significantly decreased in ECs from Gdf2/Bmp10HSC-KO mice, which further resulted in liver iron overload and disruption of HC zonation.
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining showing disappearance of glutamine synthetase in the livers of Gdf2/Bmp10HSC-KO mice (Figure 4C) and RNA-seq data showing downregulation of pericentral Wnt signal targets (Figure 4D).

claim: HSCs play a central role in mediating liver cell-cell crosstalk via the production of GDF2 and BMP10.
source: In summary, we demonstrated that HSCs play a central role in mediating liver cell-cell crosstalk via the production of GDF2 and BMP10, highlighting the important role of intercellular interaction in organ development and homeostasis.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data showing that HSC-derived GDF2 and BMP10 affect KCs, ECs, and indirectly HCs.

claim: Almost all organs in vertebrates consist of different cell types that undertake their individual functions to maintain organ homeostasis.
source: Almost all organs in vertebrates consist of different cell types that undertake their individual functions to maintain organ homeostasis (Regev et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Regev et al., 2017.

claim: Vascular endothelial cells supply oxygen and nutrients to organs.
source: such as vascular endothelial cells supplying oxygen and nutrients to the organ (Wong et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wong et al., 2017.

claim: Tissue-resident macrophages constantly clear cell debris and monitor tissue microenvironments to prevent pathogen infection.
source: and immune cells, especially tissue-resident macrophages, constantly clearing cell debris and monitoring tissue microenvironments to prevent pathogen infection (Okabe and Medzhitov, 2016)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Okabe and Medzhitov, 2016.

claim: Different cell types within organs originate from distinct progenitors and differentiate into specialized cell types via the expression of lineage-specific transcription factors during development.
source: Usually, these different cell types originate from distinct progenitors and differentiate into specialized cell types via the expression of lineage-specific transcription factors during development (Young, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Young, 2011.

claim: Crosstalk between individual cells within one organ promotes them to continue to specialize.
source: Meanwhile, crosstalk between these individual cells within one organ occurs and promotes them to continue to specialize (Pancheva et al., 2022; Armingol et al., 2021)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Pancheva et al., 2022 and Armingol et al., 2021.

claim: Cell-cell communication is needed for the maintenance of organotypic phenotypes of cells.
source: which is needed for the maintenance of the organotypic phenotypes of these cells.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge based on the preceding citations.

claim: The liver is composed of four major cell types: hepatocytes (HCs), Kupffer cells (KCs), endothelial cells (ECs), and hepatic stellate cells (HSCs).
source: The liver is composed of four major cell types: hepatocytes (HCs), Kupffer cells (KCs), endothelial cells (ECs), and hepatic stellate cells (HSCs).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about liver composition.

claim: The liver exemplifies the importance of cellular interactions in maintaining organ integrity.
source: The liver exemplifies the importance of cellular interactions in maintaining organ integrity (Monga, 2014; Ding et al., 2016; Azimifar et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Monga, 2014; Ding et al., 2016; Azimifar et al., 2014.

claim: Secretion of Wnt signaling and BMP2/6 by ECs functions on HCs to control hepatic zonation and iron metabolism, respectively.
source: For example, secretion of Wnt signaling and BMP2/6 by ECs functions on HCs to control hepatic zonation and iron metabolism (Planas-Paz et al., 2016; Yang et al., 2014; Canali et al., 2017; Koch et al., 2017), respectively.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Planas-Paz et al., 2016; Yang et al., 2014; Canali et al., 2017; Koch et al., 2017.

claim: Loss of Wnt and BMP2/6 signals results in liver dysfunction.
source: Loss of these signals results in liver dysfunction.
evidence: This is inferred from the preceding citations about the role of these signals.

claim: Recent advances in RNA-sequencing technology and algorithms have enabled a better understanding of the cellular composition and potential cellular interactions of the liver.
source: Recent advances in RNA-sequencing (RNA-seq) technology and algorithms have enabled a better understanding of the cellular composition and potential cellular interactions of the liver (Efremova et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Efremova et al., 2020.

claim: HSCs reside in the space of Disse and directly interact with HCs, ECs, and KCs.
source: HSCs reside in the space of Disse and directly interact with HCs, ECs, and KCs (Bonnardel et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bonnardel et al., 2019.

claim: HSC activation is a critical step in the development of chronic liver disease.
source: HSCs are well known for their pathological role in liver fibrosis, as HSC activation is a critical step in the development of chronic liver disease (Tan et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tan et al., 2021.

claim: ALK1 is encoded by the activin A receptor-like type 1 (Acvrl1) gene.
source: ALK1, encoded by the activin A receptor-like type 1 (Acvrl1) gene, is the receptor of GDF2 (also known as BMP9) and BMP10.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about ALK1.

claim: ALK1 is the receptor of GDF2 (also known as BMP9) and BMP10.
source: ALK1, encoded by the activin A receptor-like type 1 (Acvrl1) gene, is the receptor of GDF2 (also known as BMP9) and BMP10.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about ALK1.

claim: Mutations in ALK1 result in hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia (HHT), which causes vascular malformations in multiple organs, including the liver.
source: Its mutations result in hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia (HHT), which causes vascular malformations in multiple organs, including the liver (Miyazono et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Miyazono et al., 2010.

claim: Liver sinusoidal EC-specific Alk1-deficient mice exhibit severe liver vascular malformations.
source: It has been reported that liver sinusoidal EC-specific Alk1-deficient mice exhibit severe liver vascular malformations (Schmid et al., 2023), which mimic the liver symptoms observed in HHT patients.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Schmid et al., 2023.

claim: Liver vascular malformations in Alk1-deficient mice mimic the liver symptoms observed in HHT patients.
source: It has been reported that liver sinusoidal EC-specific Alk1-deficient mice exhibit severe liver vascular malformations (Schmid et al., 2023), which mimic the liver symptoms observed in HHT patients.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Schmid et al., 2023.

claim: ALK1 is needed for KC survival and identity.
source: We and others demonstrated that ALK1 is needed for KC survival and identity, and the ability of KCs from Alk1-deficient mice to capture bacteria from the bloodstream was significantly impaired (Zhao et al., 2022; Guilliams et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Zhao et al., 2022 and Guilliams et al., 2022.

claim: The ability of KCs from Alk1-deficient mice to capture bacteria from the bloodstream was significantly impaired.
source: We and others demonstrated that ALK1 is needed for KC survival and identity, and the ability of KCs from Alk1-deficient mice to capture bacteria from the bloodstream was significantly impaired (Zhao et al., 2022; Guilliams et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Zhao et al., 2022 and Guilliams et al., 2022.

claim: GDF2 is mainly expressed in the liver.
source: GDF2 is mainly expressed in the liver.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: GDF2 was reported to be expressed in human HCs using antibody staining.
source: Using antibody staining, GDF2 was reported to be expressed in human HCs (Bidart et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bidart et al., 2012.

claim: GDF2 and BMP10 have been shown to be mainly expressed by murine HSCs.
source: Recently, it has been reported that GDF2 and BMP10 have been shown to be mainly expressed by murine HSCs (Guilliams et al., 2022; Tillet et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Guilliams et al., 2022 and Tillet et al., 2018.

claim: Conditional deletion of Gdf2/Bmp10 from HSCs resulted in loss of KC and EC identity.
source: Interestingly, conditional deletion of Gdf2/Bmp10 from HSCs (Gdf2/Bmp10HSC-KO) not only resulted in loss of KC and EC identity but also affected HC phenotypes in an indirect way
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing loss of KC markers (Figures 1E-F) and EC markers (Figure 1G).

claim: Conditional deletion of Gdf2/Bmp10 from HSCs affected HC phenotypes in an indirect way.
source: Interestingly, conditional deletion of Gdf2/Bmp10 from HSCs (Gdf2/Bmp10HSC-KO) not only resulted in loss of KC and EC identity but also affected HC phenotypes in an indirect way
evidence: This is supported by data showing disruption of HC zonation (Figure 4C) and iron overload (Figure 4B).

claim: Conditional deletion of Gdf2/Bmp10 from HSCs resulted in liver dysfunction.
source: which ultimately resulted in liver dysfunction, suggesting that HSCs play a central role in orchestrating the interactions between different liver cell types under physiological conditions.
evidence: This is supported by data showing liver fibrosis (Figure 5B), iron overload (Figure 4B), and disrupted zonation (Figure 4C).

claim: Gdf2 and Bmp10 mRNA expression was significantly reduced in the liver tissues from Gdf2fl/flBmp10fl/flLratCre mice compared to other Cre deleter mice.
source: Quantitative PCR analysis revealed that Gdf2 and Bmp10 mRNA expression was significantly reduced in the liver tissues from Gdf2fl/flBmp10fl/flLratCre (Gdf2/Bmp10HSC-KO) mice compared to other Cre deleter mice (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: LratCre mice can specifically target HSCs.
source: Using Cre-mediated reporter mice, we demonstrated that LratCre mice can specifically target HSCs (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data from LratCreH11tdTomato reporter mice shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: BMP10 is mostly expressed in the heart, followed by the liver.
source: BMP10 is mostly expressed in the heart, followed by the liver (Neuhaus et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Neuhaus et al., 1999.

claim: Bmp10 expression in the heart was not affected in Gdf2/Bmp10HSC-KO mice.
source: However, Bmp10 expression in the heart was not affected in Gdf2/Bmp10HSC-KO mice (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data from heart tissue shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Surface markers of liver F4/80+ macrophages from Gdf2/Bmp10HSC-KO mice, including CLEC4F, Tim4, and VSIG4, were almost not expressed.
source: Accordingly, we found that surface markers of liver F4/80+ macrophages from Gdf2/Bmp10HSC-KO mice, including CLEC4F, Tim4, and VSIG4, were almost not expressed (Figure 1E and F).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence (Figure 1E) and flow cytometry data (Figure 1F).

claim: KC markers were not affected in the liver F4/80+ macrophages from Gdf2fl/flBmp10fl/flAlbCre, Gdf2fl/flBmp10fl/flTekCre, and Gdf2fl/flBmp10fl/flClec4fCre mice.
source: In contrast, these markers were not affected in the liver F4/80+ macrophages from Gdf2fl/flBmp10fl/flAlbCre, Gdf2fl/flBmp10fl/flTekCre, and Gdf2fl/flBmp10fl/flClec4fCre mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence and flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: LYVE1 and CLEC2, the surface markers of CD31+ hepatic ECs, were reduced in the livers of Gdf2/Bmp10HSC-KO mice.
source: LYVE1 and CLEC2, the surface markers of CD31+ hepatic ECs, were also reduced in the livers of Gdf2/Bmp10HSC-KO mice (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: KCs and ECs from Bmp10fl/flLratCre mice were not affected.
source: In addition, we also determined the phenotypes of KCs and ECs from Bmp10fl/flLratCre mice to exclude the possibility that the altered phenotypes observed in Gdf2fl/flBmp10fl/flLratCre mice were due to Cre-mediated cytotoxicity (Janbandhu et al., 2014) and found that these cells were not affected (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3, which serves as a control to exclude Cre toxicity.

claim: 2424 genes were differentially expressed in liver macrophages from Gdf2/Bmp10HSC-KO mice compared to their control mice.
source: We found that 2424 genes were differentially expressed (FC>2, p-adj<0.05), among which 1313 genes were upregulated and 1111 genes were downregulated in liver macrophages from Gdf2/Bmp10HSC-KO mice compared to their control mice (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by bulk RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Genes associated with the identity of KCs were significantly downregulated in liver macrophages from Gdf2/Bmp10HSC-KO mice.
source: From these differentially expressed genes (DEGs), we found that genes associated with the identity of KCs (Scott et al., 2018), such as Fabp7, Cd5l, Cdh5, and Clec4f, were significantly downregulated in liver macrophages from Gdf2/Bmp10HSC-KO mice (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2C and citation to Scott et al., 2018.

claim: Id1 and Id3, target genes of ALK1 signaling and important regulators of KC differentiation, were significantly reduced in liver macrophages from Gdf2/Bmp10HSC-KO mice.
source: Id1 and Id3, target genes of ALK1 signaling and important regulators of KC differentiation, were also significantly reduced in liver macrophages from Gdf2/Bmp10HSC-KO mice (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Embryonic KC marker Timd4 expression was downregulated in liver macrophages from Gdf2/Bmp10HSC-KO mice.
source: We also observed downregulation of embryonic KC marker Timd4 (encoding Tim4) expression and upregulation of monocytic Cx3cr1 and Ccr2 expression (Bonnardel et al., 2019; Scott et al., 2016) in liver macrophages from Gdf2/Bmp10HSC-KO mice (Figure 2D)
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2D and citations to Bonnardel et al., 2019 and Scott et al., 2016.

claim: Monocytic Cx3cr1 and Ccr2 expression was upregulated in liver macrophages from Gdf2/Bmp10HSC-KO mice.
source: We also observed downregulation of embryonic KC marker Timd4 (encoding Tim4) expression and upregulation of monocytic Cx3cr1 and Ccr2 expression (Bonnardel et al., 2019; Scott et al., 2016) in liver macrophages from Gdf2/Bmp10HSC-KO mice (Figure 2D)
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2D and citations to Bonnardel et al., 2019 and Scott et al., 2016.

claim: Embryonic KCs were lost and replaced by monocyte-derived macrophages (MoMs)/KCs in Gdf2/Bmp10HSC-KO mice.
source: suggesting that embryonic KCs were lost and replaced by monocyte-derived macrophages (MoMs)/KCs, as a reduced number of liver macrophages were observed in Gdf2/Bmp10HSC-KO mice (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is inferred from the gene expression changes and supported by immunofluorescence data showing reduced macrophage numbers in Figure 2E.

claim: A reduced number of liver macrophages were observed in Gdf2/Bmp10HSC-KO mice.
source: suggesting that embryonic KCs were lost and replaced by monocyte-derived macrophages (MoMs)/KCs, as a reduced number of liver macrophages were observed in Gdf2/Bmp10HSC-KO mice (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence quantification shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Upon KC loss, blood monocytes are recruited into the liver, immediately differentiate into F4/80+ MoMs and then gradually acquire the expression of CLEC2, CLEC4F, and VSIG4 to become monocyte-derived KCs (MoKCs) with time.
source: Upon KC loss, blood monocytes are recruited into the liver, immediately differentiate into F4/80+ MoMs and then gradually acquire the expression of CLEC2, CLEC4F, and VSIG4 to become monocyte-derived KCs (MoKCs) with time (Bonnardel et al., 2019; Scott et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bonnardel et al., 2019 and Scott et al., 2018.

claim: CLEC2 is one of the earliest markers gained by MoKCs and can be used to discriminate MoKCs from MoMs.
source: CLEC2, encoded by the Clec1b gene, was thought to be one of the earliest markers gained by MoKCs and can be used to discriminate MoKCs from MoMs (Tran et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tran et al., 2020.

claim: TREML4 expression is immediately upregulated upon blood monocyte entry into the liver.
source: In addition, TREML4 expression is immediately upregulated upon blood monocyte entry into the liver (Sakai et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sakai et al., 2019.

claim: Nearly all liver macrophages from Gdf2/Bmp10HSC-KO mice did not express CLEC2 and TREML4.
source: Interestingly, we found that nearly all liver macrophages from Gdf2/Bmp10HSC-KO mice did not express CLEC2 and TREML4, but liver macrophages from Alk1fl/flVav1Cre and Smad4fl/flVav1Cre mice did (Figure 2F)
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Liver macrophages from Alk1fl/flVav1Cre and Smad4fl/flVav1Cre mice expressed CLEC2 and TREML4.
source: Interestingly, we found that nearly all liver macrophages from Gdf2/Bmp10HSC-KO mice did not express CLEC2 and TREML4, but liver macrophages from Alk1fl/flVav1Cre and Smad4fl/flVav1Cre mice did (Figure 2F)
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The differentiation of liver macrophages from Gdf2/Bmp10HSC-KO mice is completely blocked in a status of MoMs.
source: suggesting that the differentiation of liver macrophages from Gdf2/Bmp10HSC-KO mice is completely blocked in a status of MoMs
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of CLEC2 and TREML4 expression, which are early markers of MoKC differentiation.

claim: The differentiation defect in liver macrophages from Gdf2/Bmp10HSC-KO mice is more pronounced than that from Alk1fl/flVav1Cre and Smad4fl/flVav1Cre mice.
source: and the differentiation defect in liver macrophages from Gdf2/Bmp10HSC-KO mice is more pronounced than that from Alk1fl/flVav1Cre and Smad4fl/flVav1Cre mice.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of CLEC2 and TREML4 expression between the different mouse models.

claim: Alk1 and Smad4 were efficiently deleted in KCs from Alk1fl/flVav1Cre and Smad4fl/flVav1Cre mice, respectively.
source: Our previous report has shown that Alk1 and Smad4 were efficiently deleted in KCs from Alk1fl/flVav1Cre and Smad4fl/flVav1Cre mice, respectively (Zhao et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zhao et al., 2022.

claim: Smad4 functions as a common Smad needed for transcriptional regulation in response to ALK signaling.
source: To understand this discrepancy, we performed bulk RNA-seq analysis on sorted liver macrophages from Smad4fl/flVav1Cre mice, as Smad4 functions as a common Smad needed for transcriptional regulation in response to ALK signaling.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about Smad4 function.

claim: GDF2 and BMP10 also bind ALK2 and ALK6, respectively, with low affinity to transduce signals.
source: In addition to ALK1, GDF2 and BMP10 also bind ALK2 and ALK6, respectively, with low affinity to transduce signals (Desroches-Castan et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Desroches-Castan et al., 2022.

claim: 1340 DEGs were identified between Smad4-sufficient and Smad4-deficient KCs.
source: Analysis of the DEGs between Smad4-sufficient and Smad4-deficient KCs identified 1340 DEGs, including many KC signature genes (Figure 2H and I).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figures 2H and I.

claim: 1659 of 2424 DEGs in liver macrophages from Gdf2/Bmp10HSC-KO mice did not overlap with DEGs in MoKCs from Smad4fl/flVav1Cre mice.
source: Comparison of the difference between the DEGs in liver macrophages from Gdf2/Bmp10HSC-KO and Smad4fl/flVav1Cre mice revealed that 1659 of 2424 DEGs in liver macrophages from Gdf2/Bmp10HSC-KO mice did not overlap with DEGs in MoKCs from Smad4fl/flVav1Cre mice (Figure 2J)
evidence: This is supported by Venn diagram analysis shown in Figure 2J.

claim: Alterations in other molecular mechanisms may affect the phenotypes of liver macrophages in Gdf2/Bmp10HSC-KO mice in addition to Smad4.
source: which is consistent with the phenomenon described above, indicating that in addition to Smad4, alterations in other molecular mechanisms may affect the phenotypes of liver macrophages in Gdf2/Bmp10HSC-KO mice.
evidence: This is inferred from the non-overlapping DEGs between the two mouse models.

claim: 29 transcription factors were only downregulated in liver macrophages from Gdf2/Bmp10HSC-KO mice compared to Smad4fl/flVav1Cre mice.
source: We compared the nonoverlapping transcription factors between the DEGs in liver macrophages from Gdf2/Bmp10HSC-KO and Smad4fl/flVav1Cre mice and found 29 transcription factors only downregulated in liver macrophages from Gdf2/Bmp10HSC-KO mice (Figure 2K and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by Venn diagram analysis shown in Figure 2K and data in Supplementary file 1.

claim: Rxra has been reported to regulate the development of many embryonic tissue-resident macrophages, including KCs.
source: Among these transcription factors, we focused on Rxra because it has been reported to regulate the development of many embryonic tissue-resident macrophages, including KCs (Philpott et al., 2022)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Philpott et al., 2022.

claim: RXRα deficiency significantly inhibited the differentiation of blood monocytes to MoKCs.
source: We found that RXRα deficiency significantly inhibited the differentiation of blood monocytes to MoKCs, as the proportion of CLEC2+ and VSIG4+ macrophages was significantly reduced in Rxra-deficient macrophages compared with their controls (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and C)
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data from Rxrafl/flCsf1rCre Clec4f DTR mice shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: The differentiation defect of liver macrophages from Gdf2/Bmp10HSC-KO mice may be partially caused by Rxra downregulation.
source: suggesting that the differentiation defect of liver macrophages from Gdf2/Bmp10HSC-KO mice may be partially caused by Rxra downregulation.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Rxra is downregulated in Gdf2/Bmp10HSC-KO mice and that Rxra deficiency impairs MoKC differentiation.

claim: 2692 genes were differentially expressed in ECs from Gdf2/Bmp10HSC-KO mice compared to their control mice.
source: We found that 2692 genes were differentially expressed (FC>2, p-adj<0.05), among which 1534 genes were upregulated and 1158 genes were downregulated in ECs from Gdf2/Bmp10HSC-KO mice compared to their control mice (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is supported by bulk RNA-seq data shown in Figures 3A and B.

claim: GATA4 and MAF act as master regulators of hepatic sinusoidal differentiation.
source: Both GATA4 and MAF act as master regulators of hepatic sinusoidal differentiation (Géraud et al., 2017; Gómez-Salinero et al., 2022)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Géraud et al., 2017 and Gómez-Salinero et al., 2022.

claim: GATA4 and MAF expression in ECs can be induced by GDF2 in vitro.
source: and their expression in ECs can be induced by GDF2 in vitro (Gómez-Salinero et al., 2022; Desroches-Castan et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gómez-Salinero et al., 2022 and Desroches-Castan et al., 2019.

claim: Gata4 and Maf expression in ECs from Gdf2/Bmp10HSC-KO mice were significantly reduced compared with that in their controls.
source: In our transcriptomic data, Gata4 and Maf expression in ECs from Gdf2/Bmp10HSC-KO mice were significantly reduced compared with that in their controls (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The expression of sinusoidal EC-specific markers such as Stab2, Fcgr2b, and Mrc1 was significantly downregulated in ECs from Gdf2/Bmp10HSC-KO mice.
source: Consistent with the phenotypes of Gata4/Maf-deficient ECs, the expression of sinusoidal EC-specific markers (Gómez-Salinero et al., 2022) such as Stab2, Fcgr2b, and Mrc1 was significantly downregulated (Figure 3D)
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3D and citation to Gómez-Salinero et al., 2022.

claim: The expression of continuous EC-specific markers such as Cd34, Emcn, Apln, and Aplnr was upregulated in ECs from Gdf2/Bmp10HSC-KO mice.
source: while the expression of continuous EC-specific markers (Géraud et al., 2017) such as Cd34, Emcn, Apln, and Aplnr was upregulated in ECs from Gdf2/Bmp10HSC-KO mice (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3E and citation to Géraud et al., 2017.

claim: Immunostaining revealed obviously increased expression of CD34 and EMCN, and decreased expression of LYVE1 in ECs from Gdf2/Bmp10HSC-KO mice.
source: Immunostaining revealed obviously increased expression of CD34 and EMCN, and decreased expression of LYVE1 (Figure 3F and G).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figures 3F and G.

claim: Flow cytometry confirmed the reduced expression of C-Maf, CD32b, CD117, and CD206 in ECs from Gdf2/Bmp10HSC-KO mice.
source: Flow cytometry also confirmed the reduced expression of C-Maf (encoded by Maf), CD32b (encoded by Fcgr2b), CD117 (encoded by Kit), and CD206 (encoded by Mrc1) (Figure 3H and I).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figures 3H and I.

claim: Genes associated with large arteries were significantly upregulated in ECs from Gdf2/Bmp10HSC-KO mice.
source: In addition, genes associated with large arteries (Gómez-Salinero et al., 2022) were significantly upregulated in ECs from Gdf2/Bmp10HSC-KO mice (Figure 3J).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3J and citation to Gómez-Salinero et al., 2022.

claim: Wnt pathway activation induces the expression of zonated proteins such as glutamine synthetase.

evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about Wnt pathway function.

claim: GDF2 and BMP10 play a redundant role in regulating liver metabolic zonation.

claim: PDGFB is a profibrotic cytokine that results in HSC activation and liver fibrosis.

claim: The expression of Desmin and type I collagen, two markers of HSC activation, was upregulated in the liver tissues of Gdf2/Bmp10HSC-KO mice.

claim: HSC activity was increased in Gdf2/Bmp10HSC-KO mice.

claim: Liver fibrosis in Gdf2/Bmp10HSC-KO mice was due to EC capillarization and HSC activation.

evidence: This is supported by data showing loss of KC markers and blocked differentiation at the MoM stage.

claim: Loss of GDF2 and BMP10 resulted in a shift in hepatic EC differentiation toward continuous ECs and large arterial cells.

evidence: This is supported by data showing loss of sinusoidal markers and gain of continuous EC and arterial markers.

source: Under this condition, physiological crosstalk between ECs and HCs was disrupted

evidence: This is supported by citations to Ramachandran et al., 2019; Aizarani et al., 2019; MacParland et al., 2018; Lu et al., 2022.

evidence: This is inferred from the observation that heart BMP10 expression is unchanged but KC and EC phenotypes are affected.

evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the weak ALK1 expression observed.

claim: ALK1 is weakly expressed in KCs and ECs.

evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data from Alk1tdTomato reporter mice.

claim: STAB2 expression is regulated by ALK1 signaling.
source: Indeed, our transcriptomic data showed that Stab2 expression was significantly reduced in hepatic ECs of Gdf2/Bmp10HSC-KO mice, which was consistent with the data from Gdf2 KO 129/Ola mice (Desroches-Castan et al., 2019), suggesting that ALK1 signaling regulated STAB2 expression.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that loss of GDF2/BMP10 (ALK1 ligands) leads to reduced STAB2 expression.
